A.fit: Not here: regular 28-day menses, LMP 7 days ago, cyclic pain
A.tempting: sexually active teen with pelvic symptoms

B.clue: Pelvic ultrasound to exclude anatomic obstructive anomalies
B.fit: Not here: normal pelvic exam, classic primary dysmenorrhea

C.clue: Opioid analgesia with high dependence and misuse liability
C.fit: Not here: inappropriate for cyclic primary dysmenorrhea

D.clue: Cyclooxygenase inhibition blocking endometrial prostaglandin production
D.fit: Here: regular menses, severe cyclic cramps with vomiting, normal exam

E.clue: Serotonergic antidepressant for premenstrual dysphoric disorder
E.fit: Not here: physical cyclic cramping rather than mood symptoms

nodes.text: Adolescent with recurrent lower abdominal cramping during regular menses and normal pelvic exam: primary dysmenorrhea
Pathophysiology: excessive endometrial production of prostaglandin F2-alpha causing uterine hypercontractility and ischemia
First-line therapy: nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) initiated at symptom onset or menses start
**Inadequate relief with NSAIDs after three cycles:** add combined oral contraceptive pills to suppress ovulation
**Pain refractory to NSAIDs plus hormonal contraceptives:** pelvic ultrasonography to evaluate for secondary dysmenorrhea
Encourage adjunctive therapies including local heat application and regular exercise

triggers.text: 6-month history of increasingly severe pain with menses
missed 2 days of school during each menstrual period
tender, normal-sized uterus and no masses

c-peds-04-q049.boardCall: Severe Rh alloimmune hemolysis + bilirubin 25 mg/dL + sensorineural deafness -> Exchange transfusion
c-peds-04-q049.hinge: Severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia from Rh alloimmunization exceeds phototherapy capacity and requires exchange transfusion to prevent kernicterus.
c-peds-04-q049.trap: Phototherapy was given for 2 days, but extreme bilirubin levels from severe Rh hemolysis require exchange transfusion.

A.clue: Stopping maternal milk to prevent breast milk jaundice
A.fit: Not here: severe Rh alloimmune hemolysis requires antibody removal

B.clue: Oral free water administration in neonatal dehydration
B.fit: Not here: ineffective for bilirubin reduction and causes hyponatremia

C.clue: Prolonged blue-green light phototherapy alone
C.fit: Not here: insufficient to rapidly clear extreme bilirubin 25 mg/dL

D.clue: Antimicrobial therapy for bacterial sepsis
D.fit: Not here: sterile isoimmune hemolytic disease without sepsis

E.clue: Removal of sensitized erythrocytes and unbound bilirubin
E.fit: Here: Rh-hemolysis, total bilirubin 25 mg/dL, sensorineural deafness

nodes.text: Severe Rh alloimmune hemolytic disease of newborn with total serum bilirubin >= 25 mg/dL: risk of kernicterus
Free unconjugated bilirubin crosses blood-brain barrier, depositing in basal ganglia, auditory nuclei, and brainstem
Complication: acute bilirubin encephalopathy progressing to choreoathetoid cerebral palsy and sensorineural hearing loss
Initiate immediate intensive phototherapy while preparing for emergent double-volume exchange transfusion
**Bilirubin exceeds exchange threshold or neurologic signs appear:** perform emergent exchange transfusion
**Hemolysis with rising bilirubin on intensive phototherapy:** administer intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)
Primary prevention: administer anti-D immune globulin to Rh-negative mothers during pregnancy and postpartum

triggers.text: does not appear to be startled by loud noises
mother's blood group is A, Rh-negative, and his blood group is A, Rh-positive
serum total bilirubin concentration of 25 mg/dL at the age of 2 days

c-peds-04-q050.boardCall: Pediatric DKA + orthostatic dehydration + glucose 465 mg/dL -> Administration of 0.9% saline, intravenously
c-peds-04-q050.hinge: Severe volume depletion from osmotic diuresis in pediatric DKA requires initial volume resuscitation with intravenous isotonic saline before insulin.
c-peds-04-q050.trap: High glucose and ketones tempt immediate subcutaneous or intravenous insulin, but isotonic fluid resuscitation must come first.

A.clue: Microbiologic culture to detect urinary tract infection
A.fit: Not here: emergency fluid resuscitation needed for DKA dehydration

B.clue: Oral carbohydrate challenge confirming diabetes mellitus
B.fit: Not here: contraindicated in acute diabetic ketoacidosis with glucose 465

C.clue: Glycated hemoglobin assessing chronic glycemic control
C.fit: Not here: obtain later; immediate priority is intravascular fluid repletion

D.clue: Subcutaneous insulin driving potassium and fluid shifts
D.fit: Not here: subcutaneous route poorly absorbed; give IV fluids first

E.clue: Isotonic crystalloid restoring circulating volume and perfusion
E.fit: Here: glucose 465, 3+ ketones, orthostatic hypotension, listless

nodes.text: Hyperglycemia + ketonuria + orthostatic hypotension + weight loss: pediatric diabetic ketoacidosis
Severe osmotic diuresis causes marked dehydration and intravascular volume contraction
First-line intervention: administer intravenous isotonic 0.9% normal saline bolus to restore perfusion
Start continuous intravenous regular insulin infusion only after initial fluid resuscitation is underway
**Serum potassium < 5.3 mEq/L:** add potassium to intravenous fluids before or with insulin
**Serum potassium < 3.3 mEq/L:** hold insulin until potassium is restored to prevent fatal arrhythmias
Monitor hourly neurologic status and vital signs to detect cerebral edema from rapid osmolality shifts

triggers.text: fatigue, decreased appetite, and a 2.3-kg (5-lb) weight loss over the past 2 months
blood pressure is 85/60 mm Hg while supine and 75/45 mm Hg while standing
Serum glucose concentration is 465 mg/dL

acute-leukemias.name: Acute leukemias
acute-leukemias.scope: Acute myeloid leukemia, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute promyelocytic leukemia, bone marrow biopsy, Auer rods
acute-leukemias.core: Rapid marrow replacement produces cytopenias and circulating immature cells; acute promyelocytic leukemia with coagulopathy demands immediate treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior cytotoxic treatment/radiation, benzene, myelodysplasia → AML
Down syndrome increases childhood leukemia risk; ALL predominates in children

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, fever/infections, bruising, bone pain; WBC may be high, normal or low
Hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy; T-ALL → mediastinal mass and airway/SVC compression
★ Bleeding with prolonged PT, low fibrinogen → suspect **APL-associated DIC**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Clonal immature myeloid or lymphoid expansion displaces normal hematopoiesis
Blast differentiation arrest; cell turnover predisposes to urate/phosphate release

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CBC/differential and smear → bone marrow biopsy**, flow cytometry, cytogenetics
Usually ≥20% marrow/blood blasts; defining genetic abnormalities permit some AML diagnoses below threshold
BMP, uric acid, LDH, coagulation profile; lumbar puncture for ALL CNS evaluation after stabilization

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected APL → **ATRA immediately**, then arsenic trioxide-based regimen; correct coagulopathy aggressively
Febrile neutropenia → IV cefepime; symptomatic cytopenias → blood-product support
AML → cytarabine/daunorubicin; less-fit adults → azacitidine/venetoclax; selected patients → allogeneic transplant
ALL → vincristine/steroid/asparaginase-based chemotherapy + intrathecal methotrexate; BCR-ABL-positive → add imatinib
★ Tumor-lysis prevention → hydration/allopurinol; high risk → **rasburicase**, contraindicated with G6PD deficiency

rows.label: Complications
items: Leukostasis: respiratory distress/confusion → urgent cytoreduction; tumor lysis → AKI, arrhythmias
Treatment → opportunistic infection, infertility, cardiomyopathy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Leukemoid reaction: mature neutrophilia with toxic granulation, reactive trigger
Aplastic anemia: hypocellular marrow without blast expansion

acute-leukemias.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

anaphylaxis.name: Anaphylaxis
anaphylaxis.scope: Anaphylaxis, angioedema, biphasic reactions, epinephrine autoinjector, emergency airway management
anaphylaxis.core: Rapid multisystem reaction after exposure—or isolated hypotension or airway compromise after a known allergen—requires epinephrine immediately.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Foods, insect venom, antibiotics, latex; exercise can amplify food-triggered reactions
Asthma, prior severe reaction, mast-cell disorders; beta-blockers can complicate treatment

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Urticaria/angioedema + wheeze, stridor, hypotension, or severe GI symptoms**
Skin findings may be absent; hoarseness and tongue swelling predict airway danger
Biphasic recurrence after apparent resolution, especially after severe or undertreated episodes

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mast-cell/basophil mediators → vasodilation, capillary leak, bronchoconstriction; often IgE-mediated
Epinephrine: α1 reverses vasodilation/edema, β2 reverses bronchoconstriction; albuterol alone misses edema and shock

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; never wait for tryptase or laboratory confirmation
Acute and baseline serum tryptase can support uncertain cases; normal results do not exclude anaphylaxis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **IM epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg**, adult 0.3–0.5 mg, lateral thigh; repeat every 5–15 minutes
Supine with legs elevated unless respiratory distress; oxygen, early intubation for progressive obstruction
Profound shock or refractory hypotension → titrated IV epinephrine plus **isotonic boluses**; beta-blocker use → glucagon
Albuterol for residual bronchospasm; antihistamines relieve itching only; steroids do not reliably prevent biphasic reactions
★ Monitor until resolved; **longer observation/admission** after hypotension, repeated epinephrine, or severe asthma

rows.label: Complications
items: Asphyxia, distributive shock, arrhythmia, hypoxic brain injury
Undiluted IV epinephrine bolus errors → ischemia and dangerous dysrhythmia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Prescribe **epinephrine autoinjector**, demonstrate technique, provide written action plan and allergy referral
Extra device for repeat-dose risk; avoidance, medical alert ID; venom immunotherapy after qualifying sting allergy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vasovagal episode: bradycardia, pallor, rapid improvement supine
Bradykinin angioedema: no itching/hives; ACE inhibitor or hereditary disease → airway, icatibant/C1 inhibitor

ards.name: Acute respiratory distress syndrome
ards.scope: Berlin definition, PaO2/FiO2 ratio, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema (normal PCWP), increased capillary permeability, lung-protective ventilation (low tidal volume, PEEP), prone positioning
ards.core: Acute refractory hypoxemia and bilateral opacities after a major inflammatory insult, without hydrostatic edema explaining the respiratory failure.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, major trauma, pancreatitis, near-drowning, massive transfusion
Toxic shock syndrome: renal/hepatic injury common, but **ARDS** carries the highest mortality

rows.label: Clues
items: Rapid tachypnea, increased work of breathing, diffuse crackles; oxygen requirements escalate
Severe disease: cyanosis, exhaustion, altered mentation, hypotension, multiorgan dysfunction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ★ Diffuse alveolar-capillary injury → **increased permeability**, protein-rich edema, hyaline membranes
Surfactant loss and alveolar collapse → decreased compliance and intrapulmonary shunt

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Berlin: onset **within 1 week**, bilateral imaging opacities, respiratory failure not explained by cardiac overload
ABG and FiO2 quantify severity; classification requires PEEP or CPAP ≥5 cm H2O
Echocardiography if hydrostatic edema remains plausible; PCWP generally normal, but pulmonary artery catheter unnecessary

rows.label: Tx
items: Treat precipitating cause; oxygen → intubation for severe respiratory distress or refractory hypoxemia
★ Ventilate at **6 mL/kg predicted body weight**; plateau pressure ≤30 cm H2O
★ Moderate/severe → higher **PEEP**; PaO2/FiO2 <150 despite support → prone >12 hours/day
After shock resolves → conservative fluid strategy; avoid prolonged high-pressure recruitment maneuvers
Consider corticosteroids; early severe dyssynchrony → neuromuscular blockade; refractory severe disease → VV-ECMO evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Ventilator-induced lung injury, pneumothorax, ventilator-associated pneumonia
Critical illness weakness, delirium, persistent exercise limitation; mortality often reflects underlying multiorgan failure

rows.label: Prevention
items: Aspiration precautions, infection prevention, prompt sepsis treatment; avoid unnecessary transfusions
Daily sedation assessment, spontaneous breathing trials when improving, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cardiogenic edema: elevated filling pressures, LV dysfunction, improvement with decongestion
Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage: falling hemoglobin; progressively bloodier bronchoalveolar lavage
Pulmonary embolism: hypoxemia with relatively clear imaging; CT pulmonary angiography identifies thrombus

atopic-dermatitis.name: Atopic dermatitis
atopic-dermatitis.scope: Atopic dermatitis, pruritus, flexural lichenification, emollients and topical corticosteroids, complications (eczema herpeticum, bacterial infection)
atopic-dermatitis.core: Chronic relapsing itchy eczema with xerosis; infants often have facial/extensor disease, while older children develop flexural lichenification.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Personal/family atopy, impaired skin barrier, dry climate; soaps, wool, fragrances, heat can trigger flares
Asthma and allergic rhinitis commonly coexist; scratching and bacterial colonization exacerbate inflammation

rows.label: Clues
items: Excoriations, erythema, oozing during flares; sleep disturbance and chronic thickening from rubbing
★ **Painful monomorphic punched-out erosions**, fever, rapid spread → eczema herpeticum
Honey-colored crusts, pustules, warmth or spreading erythema → secondary bacterial infection

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Barrier dysfunction increases water loss and allergen penetration; type 2 inflammation drives itch–scratch cycle

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis** by itch, distribution, chronicity; no routine serum IgE/food allergy panels
Atypical/refractory disease → assess contact allergy, infestation, immune deficiency; selected patch testing
Suspected HSV complication → lesion PCR, but begin treatment before results if clinically convincing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Daily **thick emollient**, short lukewarm bathing, fragrance-free cleanser; apply moisturizer promptly afterward
★ Flares → **topical corticosteroid**, potency by site/severity: triamcinolone on body; hydrocortisone on face/folds
Tacrolimus/pimecrolimus for sensitive sites or steroid-sparing maintenance; wet wraps for selected severe flares
Refractory moderate/severe disease → phototherapy or dupilumab; avoid chronic systemic glucocorticoids
★ Eczema herpeticum → **systemic acyclovir** now; ocular involvement → ophthalmology

rows.label: Complications
items: S aureus superinfection, disseminated HSV, sleep loss, psychosocial burden
Excess topical steroid potency/duration → skin atrophy, striae; dupilumab → conjunctivitis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Barrier care, trigger reduction, short nails; intermittent maintenance anti-inflammatory treatment at recurrent sites
No empiric elimination diets without confirmed clinical allergy; avoid routine antibiotics for uninfected eczema

rows.label: Mimics
items: Contact dermatitis: exposure-shaped distribution, patch-test association
Scabies: nocturnal household itch, burrows in webs/wrists
Seborrheic dermatitis: greasy scale, less itching

birth-trauma.name: Birth trauma
birth-trauma.scope: Caput succedaneum, cephalohematoma, subgaleal hemorrhage, clavicular fracture, facial nerve palsy (forceps compression), Erb-Duchenne palsy (C5-C6), Klumpke palsy (C8-T1), clinical course and management
birth-trauma.core: After difficult delivery, distinguish benign scalp swelling from occult hemorrhage and identify focal bone or peripheral nerve injuries.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Vacuum/forceps, shoulder dystocia, macrosomia, malpresentation, prolonged or precipitous delivery
Traction/compression can injure nerves; spontaneous delivery does not exclude neonatal trauma

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Increasing head circumference, pallor, tachycardia, poor perfusion** → concealed scalp hemorrhage until proven otherwise
Asymmetric Moro response → fracture or brachial plexus injury; inspect spontaneous movement and grasp
Clavicular crepitus/tenderness or later callus; pain-limited movement can mimic neurologic weakness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Scalp compartments differ in capacity and suture boundaries; broad potential spaces permit major blood loss
Peripheral compression causes neurapraxia; traction may produce more severe plexus disruption

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical scalp examination plus **serial head circumference and hematocrit** when bleeding suspected
Trend vitals/perfusion; CBC, coagulation studies, crossmatch for expanding swelling
Suspected fracture → clavicle radiograph if uncertain; assess joints and distinguish pain from paralysis
Facial injury: asymmetric cry and incomplete eyelid closure; examine forehead to localize peripheral palsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Shock/expanding subgaleal collection → **NICU, IV resuscitation and blood products** immediately
★ Cephalohematoma: observe bilirubin/hematocrit; **never aspirate routinely** because infection risk
Clavicular fracture → gentle handling, analgesia, brief immobilization; usually heals rapidly
Plexus injury → gentle range-of-motion/physical treatment, early follow-up; persistent deficits → specialist
Facial palsy → lubricate/protect incompletely closing eye; most compression injuries recover over weeks

rows.label: Complications
items: Blood breakdown → jaundice; massive hemorrhage → anemia, DIC, shock
Severe plexus injury → contractures and persistent weakness; corneal injury with incomplete closure

rows.label: Prevention
items: Careful instrument selection/traction, shoulder-dystocia maneuvers and team training; postinstrument delivery surveillance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Congenital muscular torticollis: sternocleidomastoid tightness rather than limb weakness
Central neurologic injury: seizures, altered alertness, broader motor abnormalities

table.title: Localization
rows: Subcutaneous edema; crosses sutures; resolves days
Subperiosteal blood; does not cross sutures; resolves weeks
Diffuse boggy expanding swelling; crosses sutures
Waiter's tip; absent Moro, preserved grasp
Weak hand/grasp; possible ipsilateral Horner syndrome

birth-trauma.evidence: Not checked online; established neonatal trauma recognition and stabilization teaching.

brain-tumors.name: Brain tumors
brain-tumors.scope: Metastatic brain tumors, glioblastoma, meningioma, pediatric tumors (medulloblastoma), vestibular schwannoma
brain-tumors.core: Progressive focal deficits, new seizures or headache with raised intracranial pressure require brain imaging for a mass lesion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Known lung, breast, melanoma, renal or colorectal malignancy → brain metastases
Prior cranial radiation; NF 2 predisposes to bilateral vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning headache, vomiting, papilledema; altered consciousness or pupillary asymmetry → impending herniation
Frontal → personality change; posterior fossa → ataxia; temporal (Meyer loop) → contralateral **superior quadrantanopia**
Pediatric posterior fossa mass can obstruct CSF flow and rapidly cause hydrocephalus
★ **Anosmia**, normal nasal exam, frontal release signs, papilledema → **subfrontal olfactory groove meningioma**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor disrupts local brain function and blood–brain barrier → vasogenic edema
Fixed cranial volume makes expanding tissue/CSF raise pressure and threaten brainstem perfusion
Astrocytoma grade, prognosis → **degree of histologic anaplasia**, not metastasis; extracranial spread rare

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Contrast MRI brain** best defines mass, edema and multiplicity; CT for unstable patients
Metastatic pattern → search primary with chest/abdominal imaging; tissue diagnosis when needed
★ Suspected mass with pressure signs → **avoid LP** until safe after imaging
Tinnitus, imbalance, facial weakness/numbness, altered taste (CN VII, V) → audiometry and MRI internal auditory canals

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic edema → **dexamethasone**; herniation → head elevation, hypertonic saline/mannitol, emergency neurosurgery
Seizure → levetiracetam; no routine antiseizure prophylaxis for every seizure-naive tumor patient
★ **Resection versus radiation** depends on lesion, symptoms, accessibility and systemic disease
Medulloblastoma → resection, chemotherapy and usually craniospinal radiation; avoid/delay radiation in very young children
Craniopharyngioma resection disrupts pituitary stalk → **lifelong pituitary hormone replacement**; watch central DI

rows.label: Complications
items: Obstructive hydrocephalus, herniation, hemorrhage, persistent neurologic deficits
Radiation injury, cognitive decline, steroid hyperglycemia and infection

rows.label: Mimics
items: Abscess: infection context and central diffusion restriction
Primary CNS lymphoma: often periventricular; steroids can obscure biopsy
Stroke: abrupt maximal onset with vascular distribution; chronic subdural: prior head trauma
Ménière disease: episodic vertigo, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss

table.title: Tumor distinctions
rows: Months of headache, deficits; necrotic, crosses corpus callosum
Woman; extra-axial, uniform enhancement, dural tail; parasagittal
Child; midline cerebellar mass; CSF drop metastases
CPA; insidious, high-frequency unilateral sensorineural hearing loss
Child; ataxia, nystagmus, head tilt, cranial neuropathies

brain-tumors.evidence: Not checked online; established neuro-oncology teaching.

child-growth-and-development.name: Child growth and development
child-growth-and-development.scope: Normal growth velocity, weight doubling and tripling milestones, WHO/CDC growth chart interpretation, developmental surveillance, normal toddler behavioral variants (head banging, temper tantrums)
child-growth-and-development.core: Interpret serial growth and developmental progress against age, family pattern, and corrected gestational age; a trajectory matters more than one percentile.

rows.label: Definition
items: Weight doubles by 4–6 months, triples by 12 months, quadruples near 24 months
Length increases about 25 cm during year 1; prepubertal height velocity about 5–6 cm/year
★ **WHO charts before 2 years; CDC charts from 2 years** in US practice

rows.label: Interpret
items: Nutrition failure: weight falls first; endocrine disease: height slows with preserved/increased weight
★ Falling **2 major percentile channels**, well child → **diet diary, calorie counts** before labs
Correct prematurity through about 2 years; track infant head circumference

rows.label: Use when
items: Developmental surveillance every visit; standardized general screens at 9, 18, and 30 months
★ **Regression/missed milestones → early intervention**; language delay → **audiometry** before speech testing
BMI-for-age from 2 years; weight-for-length younger; consider parental heights and pubertal timing

rows.label: Compare
items: Tantrums, picky eating, bedtime separation distress → reassure, routines, calm limits; no sedatives
Head banging at sleep onset or frustration, normal development → self-soothing; assess injuries
Preschool restlessness, good function → no stimulants; overwhelmed parent → **parenting classes**

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **One percentile cannot diagnose disease**; stable tracking + normal exam → reassure
Persistent skill loss needs evaluation; never wait for school failure
Short parents, normal bone age → familial; average parents, delayed puberty → **constitutional delay**

rows.label: Adolescence
items: ★ Moodiness, privacy, family detachment, rule-questioning, late bedtimes, good function → reassure, educate parents
Parental-pressure conflict, occasional experimentation, no impairment → not ODD, substance use disorder
Weight worry, stable percentile, normal BMI, regular menses → normal; not eating disorder

table.title: Normal by age
rows: Holds head up; not yet reaching
Sits unsupported; bangs blocks, self-feeds finger foods
Walks; scribbles; non-walker at 14 months normal
Balances on one foot; copies circle
Same-sex parent preference; involve other parent otherwise

child-growth-and-development.evidence: Checked screening ages 2026-10-30: [AAP surveillance/screening](https://www.aap.org/en/patient-care/developmental-surveillance-and-screening-patient-care/); growth facts established pediatric teaching.

congenital-heart-disease.name: Congenital heart disease
congenital-heart-disease.scope: Cyanotic heart disease (5 Ts: Tetralogy of Fallot, TGA, truncus, tricuspid atresia, TAPVR), acyanotic heart disease (VSD, ASD, PDA, coarctation of aorta), hyperoxia test, prostaglandin E1
congenital-heart-disease.core: Neonatal cyanosis or shock as the ductus closes demands urgent assessment for duct-dependent congenital heart disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Maternal diabetes, congenital rubella, family history; Down syndrome → AV septal defects
Prematurity → PDA; Turner syndrome → coarctation

rows.label: Clues
items: Poor feeding, diaphoresis, tachypnea, hepatomegaly → infant heart failure
VSD: harsh holosystolic lower-left sternal murmur; ASD: **fixed split S2**, pulmonic flow murmur, RV volume overload
PDA: continuous machinery murmur, bounding pulses; coarctation: weak femoral pulses, arm–leg BP gradient
Central cyanosis: blue lips/tongue, warm extremities → **low arterial saturation**; peripheral: cold extremities

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Left-to-right shunts (VSD, ASD, extracardiac PDA) increase pulmonary flow; remodeling can reverse flow → Eisenmenger syndrome
Duct-dependent lesions require pulmonary/systemic flow or mixing through fetal communications
High neonatal PVR limits VSD shunt → murmur appears/louder over weeks as **PVR falls**

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Preductal/right-hand and postductal/foot oxygen saturation; **echocardiography** defines anatomy
★ Hyperoxia test: little PaO2 rise with 100% oxygen suggests cardiac shunting; echo preferred
ECG and chest radiograph support diagnosis; normal murmur does not exclude critical disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected duct-dependent lesion → **prostaglandin E1** immediately; monitor for apnea
★ Tet spell (agitation, softer murmur) → knee–chest, oxygen, fluids, morphine; refractory → phenylephrine or propranolol
TGA with inadequate mixing → balloon atrial septostomy, then arterial switch
Large shunts → diuretics, closure; premature PDA → ibuprofen; **obstructed TAPVR → emergency repair**
Coarctation → repair; post-repair paradoxical hypertension → **IV beta-blocker**; Eisenmenger → **do not close shunt**

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary hypertension, failure to thrive, arrhythmias, infective endocarditis
Right-to-left shunting → brain abscess, paradoxical emboli, secondary erythrocytosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Pulse-ox newborn screening; rubella immunization before pregnancy; maternal glycemic control
Endocarditis prophylaxis for selected unrepaired cyanotic or prosthetic-material lesions during dental procedures

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lung disease: substantial oxygen response, pulmonary findings
PPHN: elevated pulmonary resistance with structurally normal heart

table.title: Five cyanotic lesions
rows: RV obstruction, VSD, overriding aorta, RVH; boot-shaped heart
Parallel circuits; single S2; egg-on-string silhouette
Pulmonary veins drain systemically; obstruction → edema

congenital-heart-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric cardiology teaching.

cystic-fibrosis.name: Cystic fibrosis
cystic-fibrosis.scope: CFTR mutations, meconium ileus, bronchiectasis, pancreatic insufficiency, sweat chloride test
cystic-fibrosis.core: Recurrent sinopulmonary infection plus malabsorption, poor growth or neonatal meconium ileus suggests CFTR dysfunction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autosomal recessive CFTR variants; affected sibling or carrier parents
F508del is common; genotype determines eligibility for specific CFTR modulators

rows.label: Clues
items: Chronic productive cough, recurrent pneumonia, nasal polyps, clubbing and bronchiectasis
Greasy stools, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, failure to thrive despite appetite
Salty skin, dehydration with hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis; male infertility from absent vas deferens
Neonatal abdominal distention with inspissated ileal meconium; later rectal prolapse possible

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Defective apical chloride/bicarbonate transport → dehydrated airway and pancreatic secretions
Sweat ducts fail to reabsorb chloride; pancreatic duct blockage causes exocrine destruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Positive newborn immunoreactive trypsinogen screen → **quantitative sweat chloride** confirmation
★ Sweat chloride **≥60 mmol/L** supports CF; 30–59 intermediate → repeat/genetic evaluation
Two CF-causing variants in trans or specialized CFTR-function testing resolve uncertain cases
Fecal elastase assesses pancreatic insufficiency; sputum cultures guide respiratory antibiotics
Consider CF despite negative limited mutation panel when clinical phenotype is compelling

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Daily **airway clearance**, hypertonic saline, dornase alfa; exercise supports mucus clearance
Pulmonary exacerbation → culture-directed antibiotics; Pseudomonas commonly needs antipseudomonal coverage
★ Pancreatic insufficiency → **pancrelipase with meals**, high-calorie nutrition, vitamins A/D/E/K
Eligible genotype → elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor; check liver function and interactions
Advanced respiratory failure → oxygen/ventilatory support and lung transplant assessment

rows.label: Complications
items: Pseudomonas colonization, massive hemoptysis, pneumothorax, respiratory failure
CF-related diabetes, biliary liver disease, distal intestinal obstruction, osteoporosis and infertility

rows.label: Prevention
items: Vaccination, nutrition monitoring, salt/fluid replacement during heat or exercise
Infection-control separation between CF patients; family carrier testing and reproductive counseling

rows.label: Mimics
items: Primary ciliary dyskinesia: situs inversus possible; normal pancreatic function/sweat chloride
Immunodeficiency: recurrent infection without CFTR-pattern salt loss
Celiac disease: malabsorption without bronchiectasis

cystic-fibrosis.evidence: Diagnostic threshold checked 2026-10-30: [CF Foundation sweat testing](https://www.cff.org/intro-cf/sweat-test); management established CF teaching.

dysmenorrhea.name: Dysmenorrhea
dysmenorrhea.scope: Primary dysmenorrhea, secondary dysmenorrhea (endometriosis, adenomyosis, cervical stenosis), hematometra, NSAIDs, combined oral contraceptives
dysmenorrhea.core: Painful menstruation: primary disease begins after ovulatory cycles develop; later-onset, progressive, or refractory pain suggests pelvic pathology.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Early menarche, heavy/prolonged flow, family history, smoking
Prior cervical excision/ablation → stenosis; endometriosis and adenomyosis produce secondary symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: Suprapubic cramping radiating to back/thighs, nausea, diarrhea, headache
★ **Dyspareunia, abnormal bleeding, infertility**, or pain outside menses → secondary cause
Amenorrhea or scant flow after cervical procedure with cyclic pain → retained menstrual blood

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Progesterone withdrawal → endometrial prostaglandins → uterine hypercontractility and ischemia
Outflow obstruction traps blood in uterine cavity → hematometra

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Classic adolescent presentation without red flags → **clinical diagnosis**, no initial imaging
Sexual activity → pregnancy test; infection risks → gonorrhea/chlamydia NAAT
Secondary features → pelvic examination and **transvaginal ultrasound**; transabdominal imaging if needed
No improvement after 3–6 months despite adherence → investigate secondary disease, consider laparoscopy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NSAIDs**, starting 1–2 days before expected bleeding through first 2–3 days
★ Inadequate response/contraception desired → **combined OCP** or progestin; continuous suppression may help
Heat, exercise; avoid NSAIDs with active ulcer disease or significant renal dysfunction
Treat underlying lesion; cervical stenosis with hematometra → cervical dilation/drainage

rows.label: Complications
items: School/work absence, sleep disturbance; untreated secondary disease may impair fertility
Analgesic adverse effects: GI bleeding, renal injury; estrogen-containing contraception → VTE risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Track cycles and preempt pain; ongoing menstrual suppression reduces recurrence when pregnancy not desired

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ectopic pregnancy: positive hCG, nonmenstrual bleeding, possible instability
PID: fever, mucopurulent discharge, cervical motion tenderness

table.title: Secondary patterns
rows: Posterior nodularity; ultrasound may be normal
Heavy bleeding, boggy uniformly enlarged uterus

dysmenorrhea.evidence: Not checked online; established adolescent gynecology and pelvic-pain teaching.

foreign-body-aspiration.name: Foreign body aspiration
foreign-body-aspiration.scope: Pediatric airway foreign body, choking maneuvers, rigid bronchoscopy, chest x-ray findings (air trapping, atelectasis), observation of partial obstruction
foreign-body-aspiration.core: Abrupt choking with unilateral wheeze or reduced breath sounds in a toddler suggests airway foreign body, even with normal radiographs.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Children <3 years exploring objects orally; nuts, seeds, grapes, hot dogs, toy fragments
Neurologic swallowing impairment, sedation, intoxication, poor dentition in adults

rows.label: Clues
items: Witnessed coughing/gagging during eating or play; symptoms may partially resolve after initial event
★ **Cannot speak, cough effectively, or breathe** → severe airway obstruction
Proximal obstruction: stridor; distal obstruction: focal wheeze, persistent cough, recurrent same-lobe pneumonia
Cyanosis, altered consciousness, exhaustion → imminent respiratory arrest

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Partial ball-valve blockage allows inspiration but limits expiration → distal hyperinflation
Complete bronchial blockage → resorption atelectasis; retained organic material causes inflammation and infection

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stable child → **chest x-ray**, including expiratory or bilateral decubitus views when feasible
Unilateral air trapping, mediastinal shift, collapse, or radiopaque object may identify location
Most food objects are radiolucent; negative examination/imaging does not exclude a convincing history
★ High suspicion → **bronchoscopy**; avoid delaying definitive evaluation for repeated imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: Effective cough/partial obstruction → encourage coughing, observe closely; no blind finger sweep
★ Infant severe choking: **5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts**, repeat
Age ≥1 year: cycles of five back blows/five abdominal thrusts; pregnancy/marked obesity → chest thrusts
Unresponsive → CPR, inspect mouth during airway opening, remove visible object only
★ Stable retained pediatric object → **rigid bronchoscopy** for retrieval; expert airway team for unstable obstruction

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypoxic brain injury, arrest, postobstructive pneumonia, bronchiectasis, granulation tissue
Removal can cause bleeding, edema, or pneumothorax; persistent symptoms need reassessment

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid small hard foods/toys; cut grapes lengthwise, supervise eating, avoid running with food
Teach caregivers choking response; keep small objects away from young children

rows.label: Mimics
items: Asthma: recurrent diffuse wheeze with bronchodilator response
Croup: preceding URI, barking cough, diffuse upper-airway obstruction
Bronchiolitis: viral prodrome, diffuse crackles/wheezing in an infant

gastroenteritis.name: Gastroenteritis
gastroenteritis.scope: Viral gastroenteritis (rotavirus, norovirus), foodborne illness, bacterial enteritis, traveler's diarrhea (ETEC), oral rehydration therapy, dehydration assessment
gastroenteritis.core: Acute vomiting and diarrhea usually need hydration and selective testing; shock, blood, focal pain, or systemic toxicity changes the approach.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sick contacts, contaminated food/water, travel, childcare or institutional outbreaks
Infants, older adults and immunocompromised people have greater dehydration or invasive-infection risk
Pet reptiles → nontyphoidal Salmonella; young infants prone to bacteremia

rows.label: Clues
items: Watery stools and diffuse cramps favor noninvasive disease; fever or dysentery suggests inflammatory enteritis
Mild dehydration: thirst, dry mouth, reduced urine; children → fewer wet diapers, absent tears
★ Lethargy, delayed capillary refill, tachycardia, hypotension → **severe dehydration/shock**
Toddler + high fever, bloody diarrhea, **seizure** → Shigella; HUS appears days later with hemolysis/AKI

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Intestinal secretion or epithelial injury causes water/electrolyte losses
Sodium–glucose cotransport remains functional, allowing oral rehydration despite ongoing diarrhea

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Mild self-limited illness → **no routine stool tests**
Stool PCR/culture and Shiga toxin for bloody diarrhea, high fever, severe pain or sepsis
Electrolytes/creatinine for severe dehydration; C difficile testing after antibiotics or healthcare exposure
Persistent >14 days or relevant travel → evaluate parasites; focal/peritoneal pain → imaging for surgical cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Oral rehydration solution**, frequent small volumes; continue breastfeeding and usual diet
Shock/severe dehydration or failed oral intake → IV isotonic crystalloid; reassess perfusion
Ondansetron can enable oral hydration; avoid juice/soda as primary replacement
Moderate/severe travelers’ diarrhea → azithromycin; suspected STEC → no antibiotics
Loperamide only selected adults with afebrile nonbloody diarrhea; avoid children and inflammatory disease

rows.label: Complications
items: Prerenal AKI, metabolic acidosis, electrolyte abnormalities; postinfectious lactose intolerance
STEC → HUS with hemolysis, low platelets and AKI; invasive bacteria → bacteremia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Handwashing with soap/water, food safety, **rotavirus vaccination** in infancy
Norovirus outbreaks: environmental disinfection; food handlers remain off work ≥48 hours after symptoms resolve

rows.label: Mimics
items: Appendicitis/intussusception: localized or episodic severe pain disproportionate to diarrhea
DKA: hyperglycemia, ketones; IBD: persistent bloody diarrhea and weight loss

table.title: Common noninvasive enteritis
rows: Vomiting followed by substantial watery diarrhea

gestational-diabetes-mellitus.name: Gestational diabetes mellitus
gestational-diabetes-mellitus.scope: Screening (50g oral glucose challenge at 24-28 weeks), diagnostic 3-hour 100g test, glycemic targets, nutritional therapy, insulin, fetal and neonatal complications (macrosomia, hypoglycemia, RDS, polycythemia)
gestational-diabetes-mellitus.core: Pregnancy-induced insulin resistance unmasks hyperglycemia, increasing fetal insulin secretion and growth; screen routinely at 24–28 weeks.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Obesity, prior GDM/macrosomia, family history of type 2 diabetes, PCOS
High-risk patients need early assessment for previously unrecognized overt diabetes

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually asymptomatic; excessive fetal growth or polyhydramnios may prompt evaluation
Early marked hyperglycemia suggests preexisting diabetes rather than typical later-onset GDM

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Placental hormones increase maternal insulin requirements; inadequate beta-cell compensation causes dysglycemia
Maternal glucose crosses placenta; insulin does not; fetal hyperinsulinemia persists briefly after birth
Fetal hyperinsulinemia → macrosomia; antagonizes cortisol → less surfactant, **RDS**

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Two-step screen: **nonfasting 50 g challenge**, 1-hour threshold 130–140 mg/dL by local protocol
Positive challenge → fasting 100 g, 3-hour OGTT; **≥2 abnormal values** diagnose GDM
Alternative one-step 75 g OGTT: fasting ≥92, 1-hour ≥180, or 2-hour ≥153 mg/dL
HbA1c alone does not replace pregnancy glucose testing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ First: **individualized nutrition, activity, home glucose monitoring**; avoid severe carbohydrate restriction
★ Targets: fasting **<95**, 1-hour <140, or 2-hour <120 mg/dL
Above targets despite lifestyle → **insulin preferred**; metformin crosses placenta, counsel if used
Medication need or poor control → fetal surveillance; delivery timing depends on control and obstetric findings
Suspected fetal weight ≥4,500 g with diabetes → discuss planned cesarean

rows.label: Complications
items: Maternal: preeclampsia, cesarean delivery, future type 2 diabetes
Fetal: macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, birth trauma; poor control increases stillbirth risk
Neonate: **hypoglycemia**, RDS, polycythemia, jaundice; congenital anomalies mainly reflect pregestational diabetes

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Postpartum **75 g OGTT at 4–12 weeks**; lifelong diabetes testing every 1–3 years
Breastfeeding, weight management, activity; most GDM insulin needs resolve after placental delivery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pregestational diabetes: overt diagnostic-range hyperglycemia early in pregnancy
Physiologic glycosuria: lower renal threshold without diagnostic blood glucose abnormalities

glomerulonephritis.name: Glomerulonephritis
glomerulonephritis.scope: Nephritic syndrome, poststreptococcal GN, IgA nephropathy, rapidly progressive GN (anti-GBM, ANCA), lupus nephritis, RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs, proteinuria quantification, kidney biopsy
glomerulonephritis.core: Glomerular inflammation causes hematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, edema, and reduced filtration; rapidly rising creatinine demands urgent evaluation for crescentic disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Recent streptococcal pharyngitis/skin infection, systemic autoimmunity, small-vessel vasculitis
IgA nephropathy often follows mucosal infection; anti-GBM pulmonary bleeding risk increases with smoking

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs** identify a glomerular bleeding source
Tea-colored urine, oliguria, periorbital swelling; nephrotic-range protein loss can coexist
★ **Hemoptysis + AKI** → pulmonary–renal syndrome; rapidly progressive disease may initially lack systemic symptoms

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune complexes, basement-membrane antibodies, or pauci-immune vascular injury inflame glomerular capillaries
Crescent formation compresses capillary tufts → rapid, potentially irreversible loss of filtration
Reduced filtration → sodium/water retention → **volume overload**, edema, hypertension

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Urinalysis/microscopy → **creatinine, electrolytes, urine protein/creatinine ratio**; monitor urine output
C3/C4, ANA/dsDNA, ANCA, anti-GBM; ASO/anti-DNase B when poststreptococcal disease suspected
★ **Kidney biopsy** for rapidly progressive AKI, substantial persistent proteinuria, or uncertain systemic GN
Typical childhood poststreptococcal course may not require biopsy; persistent low C3 beyond 8 weeks warrants reassessment

rows.label: Tx
items: Salt restriction, loop diuretics for overload, BP control; ACE inhibitor/ARB for persistent proteinuria when stable
★ Pulmonary–renal/RPGN → **urgent nephrology, steroids + immunosuppression** before irreversible decline
Anti-GBM: plasma exchange + cyclophosphamide; ANCA: rituximab/cyclophosphamide; plasma exchange only selected severe cases
Lupus: biopsy-directed mycophenolate/cyclophosphamide + steroids; poststreptococcal disease mainly supportive

rows.label: Complications
items: Hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, hypertensive emergency, CKD; dialysis for refractory life-threatening derangements
Immunosuppression → infection, cytopenias, infertility with cyclophosphamide

rows.label: Prevention
items: Control BP/proteinuria, avoid nephrotoxins, follow renal function and urine findings

rows.label: Mimics
items: ATN: muddy-brown casts after ischemia/toxins
Urologic bleeding: isomorphic RBCs, clots, no RBC casts

glomerulonephritis.evidence: Not checked online; established nephrology teaching.

heat-related-illness.name: Heat-related illness
heat-related-illness.scope: Heat exhaustion, classic and exertional heat stroke, malignant hyperthermia and NMS contrast
heat-related-illness.core: Heat exposure with neurologic dysfunction signals heat stroke, requiring immediate cooling before laboratory confirmation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Classic: older adults (**impaired thirst**), heat waves, impaired sweating, anticholinergics, limited water access
Exertional: strenuous activity, poor acclimatization, heavy equipment, stimulant use

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Delirium, seizures, or coma** distinguish heat stroke from uncomplicated heat exhaustion
Tachycardia, hypotension, vomiting; sweating may persist despite severe heat injury
Core temperature often >40 °C; lower readings after cooling do not exclude heat stroke

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Heat production exceeds dissipation → endothelial injury, systemic inflammation, cellular dysfunction
Sweat losses → hypovolemia; excessive free water intake can produce hyponatremia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Rectal temperature**; oral, axillary, and tympanic measurements may underestimate severity
CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, CK, urinalysis, liver enzymes, coagulation studies; repeat for evolving injury

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway support, remove clothing, **rapid whole-body cooling**; do not delay for transport or tests
Exertional: cold-water immersion, else evaporative cooling; classic: evaporative; no alcohol sponging; stop active cooling near 39 °C
★ **IV isotonic crystalloid** for hypovolemia; benzodiazepines for seizures or shivering
Avoid antipyretics; environmental hyperthermia has no elevated hypothalamic temperature set point

rows.label: Complications
items: Rhabdomyolysis, AKI, DIC, hepatic failure, ARDS, persistent neurologic deficits
Delayed liver injury despite initial clinical improvement

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Gradual acclimatization**, scheduled rest, shade, hydration, cooling access
Avoid strenuous exercise during peak heat; monitor vulnerable adults during heat waves

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sepsis: infectious focus, fever unrelated to environmental load
Serotonin syndrome: serotonergic exposure, clonus, hyperreflexia

heat-related-illness.evidence: Not checked online; established emergency medicine teaching.

herpes-zoster.name: Herpes zoster
herpes-zoster.scope: Varicella zoster reactivation, dermatomal rash, herpes zoster ophthalmicus, Ramsay Hunt syndrome, oral antivirals, postherpetic neuralgia, Shingrix vaccine
herpes-zoster.core: Latent varicella-zoster reactivation causes painful unilateral dermatomal vesicles; ophthalmic involvement or disseminated disease changes urgency and treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, HIV, malignancy, transplantation, immunosuppressive drugs
Previous chickenpox or live varicella vaccination establishes latency; no new exposure required

rows.label: Clues
items: Burning/allodynia can precede eruption by days; crops crust over approximately 7–10 days
★ **V1 distribution, nasal-tip lesions, eye pain** → urgent ophthalmology for zoster ophthalmicus
★ **Ear vesicles + ipsilateral facial paralysis** ± hearing/vestibular symptoms → Ramsay Hunt syndrome
Multiple noncontiguous dermatomes or >20 lesions outside primary/adjacent dermatomes suggests dissemination

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced VZV-specific cellular immunity permits virus to travel from sensory ganglion to skin
Neuronal inflammation/injury explains acute pain and persistent neuropathic symptoms

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical eruption → **clinical diagnosis**; atypical lesions → vesicle-base VZV PCR
Assess ocular, neurologic, and systemic findings; consider immunodeficiency evaluation for unusually severe/recurrent disease
CSF PCR for suspected CNS infection; do not delay treatment in high-risk presentations

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Valacyclovir, famciclovir, or acyclovir** ideally within 72 hours; still treat new lesions or complications
Dissemination, visceral/CNS disease, severe immunosuppression → **IV acyclovir**
Acute pain: acetaminophen/NSAID, add neuropathic agent when needed; avoid routine systemic steroids
Ramsay Hunt: antiviral plus glucocorticoid early; eye lubrication/protection for incomplete closure
Postherpetic neuralgia: **gabapentin**/pregabalin, lidocaine patch; TCA anticholinergic in elderly; no late antiviral

rows.label: Complications
items: Persistent pain >90 days, secondary bacterial infection, corneal injury, vision loss
Meningoencephalitis, vasculopathy, visceral spread in vulnerable patients

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Shingrix two doses** for adults ≥50 years or immunocompromised ≥19 years, including prior zoster
Cover lesions, **avoid susceptible contacts** until crusted; exposure causes chickenpox, not immediate shingles
Disseminated: airborne/contact until crusted; immunocompromised localized: same precautions until dissemination excluded

rows.label: Mimics
items: HSV: recurrent localized lesions, often oral/genital rather than a full dermatome
Contact dermatitis: prominent itch, exposure pattern, no neuropathic prodrome

hiv-infection.name: HIV infection
hiv-infection.scope: Acute HIV, testing, ART start, opportunistic infection prophylaxis, PrEP/PEP, opportunistic infections (CMV retinitis, toxoplasmosis, PJP)
hiv-infection.core: HIV progressively depletes CD4 cells; early diagnosis and suppressive ART prevent immune failure and sexual transmission.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sexual exposure, shared injection equipment, perinatal transmission; other STIs increase acquisition risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Acute infection 2–4 weeks post-exposure: fever, rash, sore throat, **mucosal ulcers**, diarrhea, generalized lymphadenopathy
Weight loss, thrush, recurrent candida/herpes, **extensive adult molluscum** → test HIV; dysphagia → candidal esophagitis
Child/teen: chronic fever/diarrhea, poor growth, generalized nodes, splenomegaly, **polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Retroviral integration creates lifelong reservoirs; ongoing replication drives immune depletion and inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Fourth-generation Ag/Ab → HIV-1/2 differentiation assay**; discordance → HIV RNA
★ Recent exposure/acute syndrome despite negative screen → **HIV RNA**, before antibodies appear
Baseline viral load, CD4, genotype, renal/liver function, HBV/HCV/TB, pregnancy testing, **cervical cytology**
AIDS: CD4 <200 or AIDS-defining illness regardless of count
Prenatal: opt-out screening; refusal → counsel, re-offer later; never test without consent

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Start **integrase-based ART promptly**, usually bictegravir/TAF/emtricitabine; assess HBV coinfection and interactions
Do not delay routine ART for genotype; cryptococcal/TB meningitis require disease-specific deferred timing
PJP: TMP-SMX; add glucocorticoid if PaO₂ <70 or A–a gradient ≥35
Toxoplasmosis: **pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine/leucovorin**, else TMP-SMX; CMV retinitis: valganciclovir, ophthalmology
Untreated/viremic mother's newborn → **triple ART** ASAP, ideally within 6 h, ≤6 weeks; suppressed mother → zidovudine alone

rows.label: Complications
items: Opportunistic infections, malignancies, wasting, neurocognitive disease, kidney disease
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome after ART; drug toxicity/interactions

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ PJP prophylaxis: **TMP-SMX** with CD4 <200 before/starting ART; on ART, <100 or 100–200 with viremia
Toxoplasma IgG positive + CD4 <100 → prophylaxis; MAC <50 only without immediate effective ART
★ Exposure ≤72 hours → **28-day PEP: dolutegravir + TDF/emtricitabine**; do not delay for laboratory results
PrEP: TDF/emtricitabine, cabotegravir, or lenacapavir; exclude HIV first, continue serial testing

rows.label: Mimics
items: EBV mononucleosis: atypical lymphocytes, heterophile positivity; acute HIV can be heterophile-negative
Primary CNS lymphoma: often solitary lesion; biopsy after failed empiric anti-Toxoplasma treatment, earlier if serology/imaging/CSF PCR disagree
SCID/CVID: low immunoglobulins; SCID lymphopenia, no nodes; perinatal HIV: PJP, thrush, nodes, normal lymphocytes

table.title: Advanced-disease syndromes
rows: Dry cough, hypoxemia, ground-glass; sputum/BAL silver stain
Ring-enhancing mass lesions, edema/mass effect; positive IgG
Cognitive decline; non-enhancing subcortical demyelination, no mass effect

hyperbilirubinemia.name: Hyperbilirubinemia
hyperbilirubinemia.scope: Gilbert syndrome, Crigler-Najjar, Dubin-Johnson, Rotor, unconjugated vs conjugated, biliary atresia
hyperbilirubinemia.core: Fractionate bilirubin first: indirect elevation reflects production or conjugation problems; direct elevation requires assessment of hepatobiliary excretion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Fasting, illness or dehydration triggers Gilbert jaundice; family history suggests inherited bilirubin disorders
Persistent infant jaundice can reflect biliary atresia even after initially reassuring appearance

rows.label: Clues
items: Indirect bilirubin is albumin-bound and absent from urine; direct bilirubin can darken urine
★ Infant **pale/acholic stools**, dark urine, hepatomegaly → obstructive cholestasis
Pruritus, pale stools and elevated alkaline phosphatase suggest impaired bile flow
Severe neonatal indirect elevation with lethargy, poor feeding or abnormal tone → bilirubin neurotoxicity

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Heme breakdown yields unconjugated pigment; hepatic UGT conjugation enables biliary elimination
Unbound unconjugated bilirubin crosses the immature blood–brain barrier; conjugated bilirubin does not cause kernicterus
Large hematoma/cephalhematoma resorption → bilirubin overproduction, indirect jaundice

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Total/direct bilirubin**, AST/ALT, alkaline phosphatase/GGT; CBC/reticulocytes/LDH for suspected hemolysis
Isolated mild indirect elevation with normal liver tests and no hemolysis → Gilbert diagnosis
★ Jaundice beyond 2 weeks → fractionate; **direct ≥1 mg/dL at 2–4 weeks** → urgent referral
Infant cholestasis → ultrasound; biliary atresia assessment may require biopsy and operative cholangiography
Adult conjugated elevation with pain/obstruction → RUQ ultrasound before advanced duct imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected biliary atresia → urgent pediatric hepatology/surgery; **early Kasai portoenterostomy**
Severe neonatal indirect, even Coombs-positive → **phototherapy** first; exchange: failure, critical level, encephalopathy
Crigler–Najjar I → intensive phototherapy, definitive liver transplant; type II responds to phenobarbital
Gilbert, Dubin–Johnson and Rotor → reassurance once competing pathology excluded
Cholestasis → nutritional support, fat-soluble vitamins and cause-specific treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Indirect neonatal hyperbilirubinemia → acute encephalopathy/kernicterus
Untreated atresia → cirrhosis, portal hypertension, liver failure

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Inspect stool color and fractionate persistent infant jaundice; never label conjugated jaundice physiologic

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hemolysis: anemia, reticulocytosis, low haptoglobin; newborn ABO: mother O, baby A/B, Coombs-positive
Choledochal cyst: cystic/dilated extrahepatic ducts on ultrasound
Physiologic jaundice: indirect, after 24 h, peaks days 3–5, thriving; transient UGT immaturity
Breast-milk jaundice: indirect, thriving; direct elevation excludes it

hyperbilirubinemia.evidence: Infant referral checked 2026-10-30: [AAP 2025](https://publications.aap.org/aapnews/news/pdfDownload/31302); inherited syndromes established teaching.

hyperglycemic-crises.name: Hyperglycemic crises
hyperglycemic-crises.core: Insulin-deficient diabetes with osmotic diuresis: rapid acidotic illness or slowly progressive hyperosmolar encephalopathy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Infection, missed insulin, pump failure, MI; DKA often type 1, HHS often older type 2
Euglycemic triggers: **SGLT2 inhibitors**, pregnancy, fasting

rows.label: Clues
items: Polyuria, thirst, weight loss, dry mucosa, tachycardia
DKA: abdominal pain, vomiting, **Kussmaul (deep) breathing**; HHS: profound dehydration, focal deficits
★ Severe: **hypotension, stupor**, or coma → ICU

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insulin deficit + counterregulatory hormones → lipolysis, ketogenesis; residual insulin in HHS limits ketosis
Total-body K depleted despite initially normal/high serum K

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Glucose, electrolytes, venous pH, β-hydroxybutyrate**, osmolality; ECG + trigger evaluation
Effective osmolality = 2 × Na + glucose/18; glucose in mg/dL
★ HHS: **effective osmolality >300 OR total >320 mOsm/kg**; substantial ketosis/acidosis → mixed DKA/HHS
DKA resolution: ketones <0.6 mmol/L AND (pH ≥7.3 OR HCO₃ ≥18); urine ketones/anion gap misleading

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **IV isotonic crystalloid → K correction → IV regular insulin**; K <3.5 mmol/L → delay insulin
Replace K when <5 mmol/L; glucose checks every 1–2 h, electrolytes/pH/ketones every 4 h
★ Add **dextrose** below glucose 250; euglycemic presentation → immediately; continue insulin until crisis resolves
SC basal insulin overlaps infusion 1–2 h; bicarbonate only consider pH <7.0; HHS: slower osmolar correction

rows.label: Complications
items: AKI, thrombosis; treatment: hypoglycemia, hypokalemic arrhythmias, cerebral edema (Cushing triad), hyperchloremic acidosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Sick-day fluids/ketone checks; continue basal insulin; ensure supplies and early follow-up
Hold SGLT2 inhibitors during acute illness and before surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Alcoholic ketoacidosis: binge then poor intake; usually no diabetes
Starvation ketosis: usually milder acidosis, no marked hyperglycemia
Toxic alcohols: osmolar gap, exposure; absent substantial ketonemia

table.title: Biochemistry; ketones and HCO₃ in mmol/L

hyponatremia.name: Hyponatremia
hyponatremia.scope: Hypovolemic, euvolemic (SIADH, primary polydipsia), hypervolemic, acute vs chronic, hypertonic saline indications
hyponatremia.core: Low serum sodium reflects excess water relative to sodium; symptoms and duration determine urgency before the cause determines maintenance treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Thiazides, SSRIs, carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine, oxytocin; **hypotonic IV D5W**, postoperative state, exercise + excess water
Pulmonary/CNS disease; **small cell lung cancer** (ectopic ADH); heart failure, cirrhosis, renal failure

rows.label: Clues
items: Nausea, headache, gait instability; seizures, coma or marked confusion indicate severe cerebral edema
Orthostasis/dry mucosa suggest depletion; edema/ascites suggest excess extracellular fluid
SIADH: clinically euvolemic with inappropriately concentrated urine despite hypo-osmolality
Massive water intake, often psychiatric illness; urine osmolality below serum still favors polydipsia, even if >100

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hypotonic extracellular fluid drives water into brain; chronic adaptation makes rapid correction dangerous
ADH-mediated water retention or intake exceeding renal dilution capacity lowers sodium concentration
Low effective volume (heart failure, cirrhosis, diarrhea) → baroreceptor ADH release; total-body sodium high in edema

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Serum osmolality first: **<275 mOsm/kg** confirms hypotonicity; assess glucose and volume status
Hyperglycemia → translocational hyponatremia; severe hyperlipidemia/proteinemia → pseudohyponatremia
★ Urine osmolality **<100** → polydipsia/low solute; ≥100 → persistent ADH activity
Urine Na <20–30 suggests low effective arterial volume; >30 suggests renal loss or SIADH
Exclude adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism and renal failure before diagnosing SIADH; diuretics confound urine Na

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe neurologic symptoms → **3% saline bolus**, repeated for initial Na rise 4–6 mEq/L
Hypovolemia → isotonic saline; SIADH → fluid restriction, increased solute, remove trigger
Edematous states → fluid/sodium restriction and loop diuretic; treat heart/liver/kidney disorder
★ Chronic/unknown duration: generally limit rise to **≤8 mEq/L per 24 h**; monitor frequently
Overcorrection → desmopressin plus D5W; avoid routine vaptans in acute symptomatic cases

rows.label: Complications
items: Acute severe hyponatremia → herniation, respiratory arrest
Osmotic demyelination after rapid correction; greatest risk with alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid hypotonic maintenance fluids during high ADH states; review causative drugs
Monitor for brisk aquaresis after restoring volume or stopping thiazides

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cerebral salt wasting: neurosurgical patient, hypovolemic, high urine Na; SIADH euvolemic
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemia: measured osmolality elevated
Primary psychiatric disease: neurologic change without sodium abnormality

hyponatremia.evidence: Not checked online; established hyponatremia consensus principles.

hypothyroidism.name: Hypothyroidism
hypothyroidism.scope: Hashimoto thyroiditis, subclinical hypothyroidism, myxedema coma, autoimmune associations, levothyroxine dosing, TSH monitoring
hypothyroidism.core: Insufficient thyroid hormone slows metabolism, causing fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, and delayed reflex relaxation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hashimoto autoimmunity, family history of autoimmune disease; thyroid surgery/radioiodine, iodine deficiency/excess
Lithium, amiodarone, postpartum thyroiditis; pituitary surgery/radiation or mass
Congenital primary → **thyroid dysgenesis** most common, not lymphocytic thyroiditis

rows.label: Clues
items: Weight gain, bradycardia, hoarseness, heavy menses, hyperlipidemia; hyponatremia in severe disease
★ **Hypothermia, altered mentation, hypoventilation, hypotension** → myxedema coma
Autoimmune clustering: type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, adrenal insufficiency, celiac disease
Infant: macroglossia, umbilical hernia, prolonged jaundice, hypotonia, large fontanelle → **TSH/free T4**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced hormone activity lowers thermogenesis and cardiac output; glycosaminoglycan deposition produces nonpitting edema
Hashimoto: lymphocytic infiltration; firm painless goiter, even if euthyroid; **anti-TPO/antithyroglobulin** antibodies

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TSH and free T4** establish hormone deficiency and localize the level of dysfunction
Positive anti-TPO predicts progression from subclinical disease; ultrasound unnecessary without nodule/goiter concern
Recheck mild isolated TSH elevation after transient illness resolves; exclude medication interference

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Levothyroxine**; healthy young adult approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day; older/CAD start 12.5–25 mcg/day
Fasting, apart from calcium/iron; TSH at 6–8 weeks; **persistently high → increase dose**, even if asymptomatic
Central disease: titrate using free T4; evaluate/replace cortisol before thyroid hormone
Subclinical, untreated: generally start at TSH ≥10; consider symptoms, antibodies, pregnancy at lower values
★ Myxedema: **IV levothyroxine + IV hydrocortisone**, airway support, cautious fluids/passive warming; treat trigger

rows.label: Complications
items: Dyslipidemia, infertility, pericardial effusion, neuropathy; severe disease → respiratory failure
Excess replacement → AF, angina, bone loss; rapid correction in CAD can precipitate ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Pregnancy: early **TSH monitoring**, usually increase existing replacement promptly; use pregnancy-specific targets
Monitor stable replacement at least annually; address adherence/absorption before escalating doses

rows.label: Mimics
items: Depression, dementia, psychosis: normal TSH; hypothyroidism itself can cause reversible cognitive or psychiatric symptoms
Euthyroid sick syndrome: acute systemic illness, often low T3; avoid routine hormone replacement

hypothyroidism.evidence: Not checked online; established thyroid replacement and endocrine emergency teaching.

inflammatory-bowel-disease.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
inflammatory-bowel-disease.scope: Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, extraintestinal manifestations (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, uveitis), toxic megacolon, colorectal cancer risk, biologic therapy
inflammatory-bowel-disease.core: Chronic relapsing intestinal inflammation: Crohn disease affects any gastrointestinal segment; ulcerative colitis begins in the rectum.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, young adulthood; smoking worsens Crohn disease
NSAIDs and enteric infections can precipitate flares

rows.label: Clues
items: Chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, anemia; children may have growth failure
Arthritis, uveitis; PSC particularly associated with UC
Erythema nodosum: tender nonulcerating nodules; **pyoderma gangrenosum**: rapid painful violaceous ulcer, purulent base
★ Severe colitis: fever, tachycardia, frequent bloody stools; distention, colon >6 cm → **toxic megacolon**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysregulated mucosal immune response to intestinal microbiota in genetically susceptible hosts

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stool **C. difficile** testing and cultures before attributing worsening diarrhea to inflammation
Fecal calprotectin supports intestinal inflammation; **ileocolonoscopy with biopsies** confirms
Suspected small-bowel disease or abscess → CT/MR enterography; avoid capsule with suspected stricture
Partial SBO, suspected stricture → enterography; older exam questions may expect **water-soluble small-bowel follow-through**
Fulminant colitis → abdominal radiograph and limited sigmoidoscopy; avoid full colonoscopy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute severe UC → hospitalization, **IV methylprednisolone**, fluids, VTE prophylaxis
Steroid-refractory severe UC → infliximab or cyclosporine; perforation or megacolon → urgent colectomy
★ Moderate/severe flare without obstruction or abscess → **prednisone** induces remission only; **never maintenance**
Crohn abscess → antibiotics and drainage before immunosuppression
UC with colorectal cancer → **total proctocolectomy**, not segmental colectomy

rows.label: Complications
items: Fistulas (enterovaginal → vaginal flatus), strictures, obstruction in Crohn; colectomy does not cure Crohn
Terminal ileal Crohn → B12 deficiency, **bile salt malabsorption** → steatorrhea
Colonic disease → colorectal cancer; active inflammation → venous thromboembolism

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Colonic disease → surveillance colonoscopy beginning about **8 years** after onset; PSC → immediately
Vaccinate and screen TB/HBV before biologics; smoking cessation for Crohn

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBS: no bleeding, weight loss or inflammatory markers
Ischemic colitis: abrupt pain followed by hematochezia, vascular risk

table.title: Distribution and outpatient treatment
rows: RLQ mass, cobblestones, perianal disease, granulomas
Bloody diarrhea, tenesmus; friability, crypt abscesses, pseudopolyps

innocent-murmurs.name: Innocent murmurs
innocent-murmurs.scope: Still murmur, venous hum, physiologic peripheral pulmonary stenosis, pulmonary flow murmur, benign vs pathologic features, reassurance
innocent-murmurs.core: Incidental flow sound in an otherwise healthy child; distinguish normal hemodynamics from structural heart disease using examination and positional maneuvers.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Childhood; fever, anemia, exercise, anxiety → increased flow and audibility
Prematurity favors physiologic branch pulmonary artery narrowing

rows.label: Clues
items: Soft, localized, short systolic sound; normal pulses, growth, oxygenation, S2; no thrill
★ **Diastolic, holosystolic, harsh, or ≥grade 3** → evaluate for pathology
★ Exertional syncope, chest pain, cyanosis, poor feeding, or growth failure → **cardiology referral**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Normal blood-flow vibrations without valve dysfunction, shunting, or chamber pressure overload

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Auscultation supine and standing**; assess femoral pulses, BP, family sudden-death history
Classic benign examination in older child → clinical diagnosis; routine ECG/CXR add little
Uncertain findings or persistent neonatal murmur → pediatric cardiology; **echocardiography** defines structural lesions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Reassurance**; unrestricted sports and usual childhood activities
No cardiac drugs, endocarditis prophylaxis, or serial imaging after confident benign diagnosis

rows.label: Complications
items: No heart failure or progression to structural disease; mistaken labeling → anxiety and unnecessary activity restriction

rows.label: Mimics
items: ASD: fixed split S2; pulmonary stenosis: ejection click
PDA: unvarying machinery sound; bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: louder with standing or Valsalva; concerning family history

table.title: Benign patterns
rows: Disappears supine or with jugular compression

juvenile-idiopathic-arthritis.name: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis
juvenile-idiopathic-arthritis.scope: Oligoarticular JIA, polyarticular JIA, systemic JIA, uveitis screening, NSAIDs, methotrexate
juvenile-idiopathic-arthritis.core: Persistent childhood inflammatory arthritis is a diagnosis of exclusion; silent eye disease and systemic inflammatory complications require active surveillance.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Onset before age 16; female predominance in oligoarticular/polyarticular forms
Young onset, ANA positivity and oligoarthritis increase chronic anterior uveitis risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Morning stiffness, swollen joints or painless limp** persisting ≥6 weeks
Limited range of motion, warmth, leg-length difference; child may avoid activity rather than report pain
Systemic inflammation with falling platelets, hepatic dysfunction or altered mentation → macrophage activation syndrome

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune-mediated synovitis → cartilage damage and altered growth
Systemic form predominantly autoinflammatory, involving IL-1 and IL-6 pathways

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis after excluding infection/malignancy**; CBC, ESR/CRP, ANA, RF by phenotype
ANA predicts eye risk rather than proving arthritis; RF often negative
Acutely hot painful joint with fever → arthrocentesis/culture before attributing to JIA
Suspected macrophage activation → ferritin, triglycerides, fibrinogen, CBC and liver enzymes

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Oligoarthritis → **NSAIDs or intra-articular glucocorticoid**; persistent disease → methotrexate
Polyarthritis → methotrexate; uncontrolled disease → biologic such as TNF inhibitor
★ Systemic JIA → **IL-1/IL-6 inhibitor** such as anakinra/tocilizumab; limit chronic systemic steroids
Uveitis → topical ocular steroid, then methotrexate/adalimumab for persistent disease; avoid etanercept for ocular control
Physical rehabilitation, range-of-motion exercises and nutrition support

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic uveitis → cataract, glaucoma, vision loss without symptoms; joint destruction and growth disturbances
Macrophage activation → cytopenias, coagulopathy, multiorgan failure; immunosuppression → infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Slit-lamp screening**, every 3 months in high-risk children, even without eye complaints
Vaccination review, TB screening before biologics; monitor methotrexate CBC/liver tests

rows.label: Mimics
items: Septic arthritis: abrupt severe monoarthritis, bacterial culture
Leukemia: nocturnal bone pain, cytopenias/blasts; reactive arthritis: follows infection, usually self-limited
Acute rheumatic fever: recent strep, migratory arthritis, carditis, nodules; not persistent single-joint swelling

lyme-disease.name: Lyme disease
lyme-disease.scope: Borrelia burgdorferi, erythema migrans, early localized, early disseminated, late Lyme arthritis, doxycycline, ceftriaxone
lyme-disease.core: Ixodes-transmitted Borrelia infection progresses from an expanding skin lesion to neurologic, cardiac, or joint disease when untreated.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Wooded/brush exposure in Northeast, mid-Atlantic, upper Midwest; attached blacklegged tick
Tick exposure may be unnoticed; small-mammal reservoirs sustain transmission

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Erythema migrans**: enlarging lesion >5 cm, days after bite; central clearing not required
Early dissemination: multiple lesions, unilateral/**bilateral facial palsy**, lymphocytic meningitis, fluctuating AV block
Late disease: intermittent large-joint swelling, especially knee; severe pain less prominent than effusion

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Spirochete inoculation → local multiplication, hematogenous spread, inflammatory injury
Persistent antibodies can remain after cure and do not prove viable infection

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical erythema migrans → **clinical diagnosis**, no serology needed
Other compatible disease → two-tier serology: EIA followed by immunoblot or second EIA
Early localized serology may be negative; isolated IgM after >30 days is unreliable
Joint-fluid PCR supports selected arthritis cases; CSF testing for CNS disease; ECG for cardiac symptoms

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Localized skin disease → **doxycycline 10 days**, or amoxicillin/cefuroxime 14 days
Facial palsy/mild neurologic disease may use oral doxycycline; severe CNS disease → IV ceftriaxone
★ Symptomatic carditis, PR ≥300 ms, higher-degree block → **hospitalize, telemetry, IV ceftriaxone**; pacing if needed
Lyme arthritis → 28-day oral course; persistent objective disease requires reassessment, sometimes IV ceftriaxone
Post-treatment nonspecific fatigue → supportive evaluation; no prolonged antibiotics without objective reinfection/failure

rows.label: Complications
items: Complete heart block, meningoencephalitis, recurrent arthritis, postinfectious joint inflammation
Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction shortly after antibiotics; not necessarily drug allergy

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ High-risk Ixodes bite, attachment ≥36 hours, endemic region → **single-dose doxycycline within 72 hours of removal**
Tick checks, permethrin-treated clothing, DEET; remove tick with fine tweezers near skin
No prophylaxis for low-risk bite or routine serologic testing of asymptomatic patients

rows.label: Mimics
items: Immediate bite hypersensitivity: small, itchy, does not progressively enlarge
Septic arthritis: marked pain, toxicity, positive culture; babesiosis: hemolysis and intraerythrocytic parasites
Neurosyphilis: Lyme can falsely react on syphilis serology; tick exposure + facial palsy → Borrelia antibodies

meningitis.name: Meningitis
meningitis.scope: Bacterial meningitis, viral meningitis, fungal/cryptococcal meningitis, CSF interpretation, empiric antimicrobial therapy, chemoprophylaxis
meningitis.core: Fever, headache and meningeal symptoms require prompt CSF evaluation when safe; suspected bacterial meningitis demands antibiotics without imaging-related delay.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Adults: **S. pneumoniae** most common; seeded by pneumonia, otitis, sinusitis, CSF leak, asplenia
Neonates: GBS, E. coli, Listeria; older adults/immunocompromised: additional Listeria risk
Crowding/asplenia → meningococcus; advanced HIV/transplant/chemotherapy → Cryptococcus

rows.label: Clues
items: Neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting; infants may show poor feeding, irritability or bulging fontanelle
★ Petechiae/purpura with shock → **meningococcemia**; absence of rash does not exclude
Confusion, seizure or focal deficit raises encephalitis, raised-pressure or complicated infection concern

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Organisms reach meninges hematogenously or through contiguous spread/CSF defect; inflammation increases edema and pressure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Blood cultures → LP** with opening pressure, cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain/culture and PCR
CT before LP for focal deficit, papilledema, new seizure, marked consciousness impairment or significant immunocompromise
★ If LP delayed: cultures then **immediate antibiotics**; CT cannot rule out every pressure hazard
Cryptococcus: subacute, high opening pressure ± CN VI palsy, CSF antigen; TB studies if lymphocytic, low glucose

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Adult empiric → **vancomycin + ceftriaxone**; add ampicillin if >50 or immunocompromised
Neonate → ampicillin + cefotaxime; avoid ceftriaxone in neonates
Dexamethasone before/with first antibiotic when pneumococcal meningitis suspected; narrow treatment by organism
Cryptococcal meningitis → liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine, then fluconazole; serial therapeutic LPs for pressure
Uncomplicated viral meningitis → supportive care; suspected HSV encephalitis → IV acyclovir

rows.label: Complications
items: Hearing loss, seizures, hydrocephalus, stroke, cognitive impairment; meningococcus → DIC/adrenal hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Meningococcal contacts within 7 days of onset → **rifampin or ceftriaxone**; droplet isolation until 24 hours treated
Hib prophylaxis for qualifying households/childcare; no routine pneumococcal contact antibiotics
Pneumococcal, Hib and meningococcal vaccination; correct recurrent CSF leaks

rows.label: Mimics
items: SAH: thunderclap headache; CT/LP hemorrhagic findings
Encephalitis: parenchymal dysfunction, focal deficits or prominent behavioral change

meningitis.evidence: Contact prophylaxis checked 2026-10-30: [CDC meningococcal guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/surv-manual/php/table-of-contents/chapter-8-meningococcal-disease.html); empiric regimens established teaching.

methemoglobinemia.name: Methemoglobinemia
methemoglobinemia.scope: Oxidizing agents (dapsone, benzocaine, nitrates), chocolate-brown blood, pulse oximetry saturation gap, PaO2 normal, methylene blue, vitamin C
methemoglobinemia.core: Cyanosis that barely improves with oxygen despite adequate dissolved arterial oxygen suggests dysfunctional hemoglobin rather than primary lung failure.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ Oxidants: **dapsone, benzocaine, nitrates/nitrites**; also prilocaine and some industrial chemicals
Infants exposed to nitrate-contaminated well water; congenital cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Chocolate-brown blood**, gray-blue skin, pulse oximeter trending toward ~85%
Headache, dizziness, tachycardia, dyspnea; severe exposure → confusion, seizures, arrhythmias, coma
Symptoms occur at lower levels with anemia or cardiopulmonary disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hemoglobin iron oxidized Fe2+ → Fe3+; oxidized sites cannot bind oxygen
Remaining functional sites bind oxygen more tightly → impaired tissue unloading

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Co-oximetry** directly measures methemoglobin fraction; obtain venous or arterial blood
